![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095212/assets/56923d0bc8f47d504837e3dca2f7191cf3d5d571245ee4453c8d1272dfb1dbd3.png)
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find a $3\times 3$ matrix that could be the matrix $U.$
examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $\Sigma$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3 \times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=\sqrt5$ and $\sigma_2=0.$ 
Also, the columns $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, and we do not have a third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095212/assets/adcd255d41a153210074a9ce091f40a65faeea884f2462275058ddf057b821f6.png)

such that $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0$ and $\|\mathbf{u}\|=1.$

Solving $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} x_1 + \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} x_2 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_1 + 2x_2 = 0,
$$

we get the general solution 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095212/assets/cb7815fe5b5010a29a93a97bede16e26a7a0382a0d8c8f1c2a3af85762d24f00.png)

where $x_2$ and $x_3$ are free variables. Notice that the two linearly independent solutions are mutually orthogonal. Normalizing these vectors, we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095212/assets/bbbb111ac90a0d42ab31aa78b0e36d2bdd00436e9f0fbabde2342120f32e1120.png)

Finally, we construct the matrix $U \mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095212/assets/c348424c58cf218e1e4fc0eb3c3efa27517c6a24ac786146f0543f945f31af33.png)

feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}=0,\end{aligned}
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$
